bio.en: Adam Grenier is a growth and marketing leader who built Uber's growth marketing team and infrastructure from scratch, served as VP of Product and Marketing at Lambda School and VP of Marketing at MasterClass, and now advises companies and invests while shaping the emerging "Growth CMO" model.
bio.zh: Adam Grenier 是一位增长与营销领导者，曾在 Uber 从零搭建增长营销团队与基础设施、担任 Lambda School 产品与营销 VP 及 MasterClass 营销 VP，如今作为顾问和投资人在新兴获客渠道与「增长型 CMO」理念上影响行业。

summary.en: Adam lays out a three-ingredient framework for evaluating emerging acquisition channels: overlap between the channel's strengths and your customer and business needs (a green light only if they align), the channel's DNA (its stage and monetization strategy—matching theirs earns you an edge), and your own company DNA (risk appetite and existing channel mix). He advises testing with minimal resources, treating it like "fishing" and not letting it bleed past a quarter, noting only ~5% of new channels truly pan out. On the "Growth CMO," he argues product and marketing must be married at the hip and run with an agile, experimental mindset—traditional CMOs often fail because of that mismatch. He closes with a candid mental-health arc: burnout is often actually depression, distinguishable by whether you still show up for what you love, and therapy, a supportive partner, transparent friends, and meditation are what got him through.
summary.zh: Adam 提出评估新兴获客渠道的「三要素框架」：媒介优势是否与客户需求和公司目标重叠（重叠才亮绿灯）、渠道的 DNA（所处阶段、变现方式，匹配对方变现策略能拿到先发优势）、以及公司自身 DNA（风险偏好与现有渠道组合）。他建议用最小资源先「钓鱼」测试、别拖过一个季度，并提醒真正跑通的渠道只有约 5%。关于「增长型 CMO」，他认为产品与营销必须绑在一起、用敏捷和实验心态运作，传统 CMO 常因不匹配而失败。最后他坦诚分享心理健康历程：倦怠常其实是抑郁，区分在于你是否还愿意投入热爱的事；therapy、伴侣、透明朋友圈和冥想是撑过来的关键。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: One of the biggest pieces of advice I'm giving to people that are like, "How should we adjust our marketing with the economic changes and things like that?" I was like, "Start by assuming you no longer have product market fit, because you had product market fit in a different market." It's a different market now, so you have to start over. And hopefully you do, or it's pretty close to it and you just have to adjust a couple things, and you could be right back on track. But if you just assume you need to launch a new channel to fix this problem, you're going to be wrong, because your entire customer base changed, not just the next 10% of customers that you're looking for.
turns.zh: 我给那些问「经济变化了，我们该怎么调整营销？」的人的最大一条建议是：「先假设你们已经没有产品市场契合了，因为你是在一个不同的市场里获得的产品市场契合。现在市场不一样了，所以你得从头来。」希望你是这样，或者离那很近、只要调几样就能重回正轨。但如果你只是假设「我需要上线一个新渠道来修这个问题」，那你就错了，因为你的整个客户群都变了，不只是你找的下一个 10% 的客户。

turns.en: Adam, welcome to the podcast.

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sound good?
turns.zh: 可以吗？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 可以。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so you were most recently VP of Marketing at Masterclass, which I'm actually a happy subscriber of and I've watched many a video. Before that, you were VP of Product and Marketing at Lambda School. I don't know if that's right before, but that was something you did. And I think you spent four years there and you basically built their growth marketing infrastructure and the team. And currently you're doing a bunch of advising and exploring to see what you want to do next. Is that about right?
turns.zh: 好，你最近是 MasterClass 的营销 VP，我其实是个满意的订阅者，看过很多视频。之前你是 Lambda School 的产品和营销 VP。我不知道是不是紧挨着之前，但那是你做过的事。还有，你是 Uber 的增长营销与创新负责人，头衔很酷。我想你在那待了四年，基本从零搭建了他们的增长营销基础设施和团队。现在你在做一堆顾问和探索，看下一步想干啥。差不多吧？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Yeah, you hit most of the key points. I think pre-Uber, the first chunk of my career was on the advertising side, so worked in agency world. So, I kind of think of this as phase three of my life. Ads world was phase one, startup and growth world phase two, and now really just spending time helping entrepreneurs and founders and built companies and that type of stuff.
turns.zh: 对，关键点你差不多都点到了。Uber 之前，我职业生涯前半段在广告这边，在广告公司干过。所以我把它想成我人生的第三阶段。广告世界是第一阶段，创业和增长世界是第二阶段，现在就是花时间帮创业者、创始人和已建成的公司这类事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's been your favorite phase so far?
turns.zh: 目前为止你最喜欢哪个阶段？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: I mean all of them. I just embrace what gets thrown at me and allow it to organically happen. So, each phase has had its pros and cons and ups and downs, and so I think they've all fit pretty well into where I was in my career.
turns.zh: 都挺好。我就是拥抱扔到我面前的东西，让它自然发生。所以每个阶段都有利弊和起伏，我觉得都挺契合我当时在职业生涯的位置。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of moving and adjusting and iterating, I know you're big into improv. How serious are you about improv?
turns.zh: 说到转变、调整和迭代，我知道你很迷即兴表演（improv）。你对 improv 有多认真？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Good question. Serious in the sense that I've done it for a very long time and I still do it and I try to do it regularly. Serious as in am I aiming to make money off of it and have a career out of it? Unfortunately not. There was a point in my life that that is what I wanted to do. I lived in Chicago, did Second City ImprovOlympic, a variety of different places, did quite a bit of performing, but also got into corporate paychecks early as well.
turns.zh: 好问题。认真在于我做这个很久了，现在还在做，也尽量定期做。认真在于我要不要靠它赚钱、把它当职业？可惜不是。我人生有段时间是想这么干的。我住在芝加哥，待过 Second City、ImprovOlympic 等各种地方，演了不少，但也很早就开始拿公司工资了。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: And so kind of built a lifestyle that made doing improv full time probably not the best path for me at the time. And so made a pretty conscious choice early on that it was more of a hobby and if something ever came of it, cool, but if not, that's okay. It's something I keep coming back to, because it's very grounding and fulfilling in ways that work and family life and things like that don't quite hit for me.
turns.zh: 所以某种程度上我把生活过成让全职做 improv 在当时可能不是最好的路。所以很早我就很自觉地把它当成爱好，如果哪天有结果，很酷，但没有也无所谓。我会一直回到它，因为它在工作和家庭生活之类打不到我的地方，给我踏实和满足。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Actually at Airbnb we had an improv teacher come and work with the PM team. It was for months. We did improv games once a week.
turns.zh: 其实在 Airbnb 我们有个 improv 老师来跟 PM 团队一起工作。搞了几个月。我们一周玩一次 improv 游戏。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Nice.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And played all these fun things. And I'm curious what you've taken away from improv that has helped you become better at your work?
turns.zh: 玩了所有这些好玩的。我很好奇，你从 improv 里学到了什么，帮你把工作做得更好？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: So, I think generally the whole suite of skills that you develop in improv are pretty applicable, right? Because you are getting comfortable on your feet with change, with teamwork, building off of each other, experimenting, trying new things, a little bit of everything. I think a couple of the key rules or themes of improv that I really try to hammer home with people are obviously the "Yes, and..." side of improv, which everyone's probably heard, which is in a scene the worst thing you could do is deny somebody, because you're actually just stopping progress and you're not building off of anything.
turns.zh: 我觉得 generally，你在 improv 里发展出来的整套技能都挺适用的，对吧？因为你变得更适应在变化中、在团队里临场发挥，互相搭建、做实验、试新东西，什么都有一点。我觉得 improv 里几个关键规则或主题，我真的很想让人记住，显然就是「Yes, and...」（好，而且……），这个大家都听过——在一个场景里你能做的最糟的事是否定别人，因为你其实就是在停止推进、没有在任何东西上搭建。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: So, the appropriate approach is to say, "Yes, that is true, and..." and add to it. So, if someone's like, "Hey, you have a chicken on your head," not saying, "No, I don't." Just kind of ruins that scene. Versus saying, "Yes, I do, and it's name is Sally. What's your chicken's name?" Builds on that and gives it more opportunity. And so I think that in growth in business is super important to be able to say, "Yes, I do see your idea," or "Yes, we did accomplish this and this is what we want to do next and this is how it's going to build on it," I think is super important.
turns.zh: 所以正确的方式是说「对，那是真的，而且……」然后加上去。所以如果有人说「嘿，你头上有只鸡」，不要说「不，我没有」。那直接毁了那个场景。而说「对，我有，它叫 Sally。你的鸡叫什么？」就在上面搭起来，给了更多机会。所以我觉得在增长和生意里，能说「对，我确实看到你的想法」或者「对，我们确实达成了这个，这是我们接下来想做的，这是它怎么搭上去的」超级重要。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: The other one that I think is less known or talked about is the gift of details. So, in a scene, if you give somebody really specific details about something, it gives so much more meat to be able to work off of in terms of what's coming next. So, if someone's starting a scene and they're clearly watching television and clicking through the channels and I walk up and just say like, "Oh, you're watching TV, cool." That's a yes statement. I'm not denying what they did. But if I come up and say like, "Oh cool, you're watching TV. Is that an Alf episode? I haven't seen Alf since I was a kid. It reminds me this one time I actually ate my own cat."
turns.zh: 另一个我觉得比较少人知道或谈的是「细节的礼物」。在一个场景里，如果你给别人非常具体的细节，就给了特别多料，能接着往下发展。所以如果有人起一个场景，明显在看电视、换台，我走过去只说「哦，你在看电视，酷」。那是个 yes 陈述。我没否认他做的。但如果我走过去说「哦酷，你在看电视。是 Alf 那一集吗？我小时候之后就没看过 Alf 了。它让我想起有一次我真的吃了自己的猫。」

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Just giving those specific details of Alf and me as a kid and I had a cat, which if people don't know Alf, he ate cats.
turns.zh: 就给那些具体的细节——Alf 和我小时候、我有只猫（不了解的人可能不知道，Alf 吃猫）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't remember that. I remember Alf, but I don't remember he ate cats.
turns.zh: 我不记得那个。我记得 Alf，但不记得他吃猫。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: He was always trying to get the family cat. So, those kinds of details add a ton of value and you take that into the business world, to use Masterclass for instance, if I say, "Yeah, Masterclass, we've got this way to build content that is both entertainment and education," that's interesting. But if I say, "We create content that is both education and entertainment to solve people's deep curiosities in the way that maybe a biography would." That just opens up the exact problem that you're trying to solve. What are other alternatives to that problem? How are people consuming that? So, I think the gift of details in good improv and learning those skills is something that I really value and look for in every aspect of my business life as well.
turns.zh: 他一直想抓那家的猫。所以这类细节加了超多价值，你把它带到商业世界，比如用 MasterClass 举例，如果我说「对，MasterClass，我们有种做内容的方式，既是娱乐也是教育」，那挺有意思。但如果我说「我们做的内容既是教育也是娱乐，去解决人们深层的好奇心，就像一本传记会做的那样」。那正好打开了你想解决的确切问题。那个问题还有什么别的替代解法？人们怎么消费它？所以我觉得好的 improv 里「细节的礼物」、以及学这些技能，是我在生意生活的每个方面都真的很看重、也去寻找的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It sounds like it's really helpful, one, in marketing, creativity and positioning, and things like that you just described. Have you found it also to be helpful in collaboration like this "Yes, and..." piece? I'm curious, is there an example or story where you like "Yes, and..." someone? Do you actually say "Yes, and..." in a meeting? How do you actually find that you use it?
turns.zh: 听起来它真的很有用，一是在你刚描述的营销、创意和定位上。你发现它在协作上也有用吗，就像「Yes, and...」这块？我好奇，有没有例子或故事是你「Yes, and...」了某人的？你会在会上真的说「Yes, and...」吗？你实际是怎么用它？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: I hear it every now and then. I don't usually literally say it. I think one of the areas that I've found it to be valuable is when you've got cross-functional work. So, obviously at Uber we dealt with city teams a lot, and so a lot of the times the way that the central team would scope a problem versus a local team would scope a problem, would almost feel at odds with each other. And if you approach it with that "Yes, and...", it's often still true.
turns.zh: 我偶尔听到。我通常不照字面说。我觉得它有价值的一个领域是跨职能工作。显然在 Uber 我们常跟城市团队打交道，所以很多时候中央团队怎么框定一个问题、跟本地团队怎么框定，几乎像在对着干。如果你用「Yes, and...」的方式，它常常还是成立的。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: It's like, oh, both of these things can be true at once. You could have a different goal than I have, or you have a system problem local to you that is important to you and it's not important to me. That's okay, both things can exist. So, now that we accept both and can work off of each other, we're more likely to build both a better rapport and energy among ourselves because we're not just saying, "No, no, no, no, you're wrong. That's not true, that's not important to the business. Why are you doing that?" That type of energy when cross-functional work, it just kills the scene, it kills that progress. And then you don't build relationships, you don't build the right solutions, all that type of stuff.
turns.zh: 就像是，哦，这两件事可以同时为真。你可以有跟我不同的目标，或者你有个对你很重要的本地系统问题、而它对我不重要。那没事，两件事可以共存。所以既然我们都接受、能互相搭建，我们就更可能建立更好的 rapport 和我们之间的能量，因为我们不是只说「不不不不，你错了。那不对，那对生意不重要。你干嘛做那个？」那种能量在跨职能工作里，就是毁了场景、毁了进展。然后你不建立关系、不建立对的方案，所有那些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It sounds really good. Everyone in theory wants to be really good at this. And I imagine just doing a bunch of improv is a really good way to get better at not getting defensive and being like, "Yes. And how do we make this idea better?" Is there something you can advise folks to work on this skill, or is it just do a bunch of improv classes and it'll kind of help build that skill?
turns.zh: 听起来真不错。理论上每个人都想很擅长这个。我猜多做一些 improv 就是变好、不那么防御、变成「对。那我们怎么把这个想法变得更好？」的好办法。你有什么建议给大家练这个技能吗，还是就是去上一堆 improv 课、它就会帮你建起那个技能？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: That's one. I would say that I'll say that all the time to people, "Do some improv classes." And I get a lot of people like, "No, I'm not funny," or, "I don't want to do improv." And I think it's still a really great class to take, even if you have zero interest in doing improv, or public speaking, or any of that kind of stuff. Because, again, improv 101 is taught everywhere. Every city has it somewhere, and it's rarely ever people that are trying to do improv professionally. It's all games, like you said. The classes that you all did at Airbnb is what improv 101 is, right?
turns.zh: 那是一个。我会一直跟人说「去上点 improv 课」。然后很多人说「不，我不搞笑」或者「我不想做 improv」。我觉得就算你对做 improv、公开演讲之类零兴趣，它还是门超棒的课。因为，再说一遍，improv 101 到处都教。每个城市某处都有，而且极少是冲着专业做 improv 的人。全是游戏，就像你说的。你们在 Airbnb 上的那些课就是 improv 101，对吧？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: It's just like, "Hey, let's just have fun. Let's just get out of our skin," and things like that. So, I do think everybody should take improv classes. I think it's also something with a lot of goals or skills that you want to develop, I think being really public and open about you wanting to develop that. So, if you are managing a team and you want to sharpen the skills, make it a team goal, or have accountability and just say, "Hey guys, I know that I've been pushing back on things lately. I want to really try to embrace and grow off of ideas better, hold me accountable, call me out and be like, 'Adam, "Yes, and..." this please."
turns.zh: 就是「嘿，我们玩得开心点。跳出自我」之类。所以我确实觉得每个人都该上 improv 课。我也觉得，对任何你想发展的目标或技能，很公开、很坦诚地说你想发展它，也很重要。所以如果你带一个团队、想磨这个技能，把它变成一个团队目标，或者搞问责，就说「嘿哥们，我知道我最近一直在 push back，我真的想更好地接纳想法、从想法上成长，盯着我点，就说『Adam，请 "Yes, and..." 这个』」。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Or giving people permission to push back on that when it doesn't happen, I think also just opens the door for more productive conversations with people and the ability to hold yourself accountable and keep trying it.
turns.zh: 或者给大家权限，在没做到的时候 push back 这个，我觉得也打开了更高效的对话之门，让你能问责自己、持续尝试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. And such a good team bonding activity. There's like all these reasons to do this as a team. My wife actually, she's a designer, artist, writer, illustrator kind of person, and she's been taking a lot of these sorts of classes to help inspire her creativity. She never wants to be an improv person, she did stand up classes.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。而且是个很好的团队 bonding 活动。有太多理由作为团队去做这个了。我老婆，她是个设计师、艺术家、作家、插画师那种人，她上了很多这类课来激发创意。她从不想当 improv 的人，她上了单口喜剧课。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: That's awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As you said, it just helps you get the juices flowing along these lines. Okay, so we're not going to talk about improv the whole time.
turns.zh: 如你说的，它只是帮你沿着这些线把 juices 流动起来。好，我们不会整个聊 improv。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: We could if you want to.
turns.zh: 想聊也行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We could. Throw me word, let's go. No, we don't want to do that. So, there's basically three things I really wanted to chat about with you. One is how to decide when to invest in an emerging acquisition channel like TikTok, VR, Clubhouse was a big thing. You have some really interesting thoughts on how to decide and approach this thing. To the growth CMR role, which is kind of this, I think emerging role, something you're really good at, and I just want to get your thoughts on what's happening there. And then, three, some real talk on burnout and depression that often comes with working in tech and stuff that we go through. Does that sound good?
turns.zh: 可以。给我个词，走。不，我们不想那样。所以，基本有三件事我特想跟你聊。一是怎么决定什么时候去投资一个新兴的获客渠道，比如 TikTok、VR、Clubhouse 当时很火。你对怎么决定、怎么接近这事有很有意思的想法。二是增长型 CMO 角色——我觉得这是个新兴角色，你特别擅长，我想听听你对那在发生什么的想法。三是一些关于倦怠和抑郁的真心话，那是科技行业和我们一起经历的事常带来的。可以吗？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 可以。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. So, to start with in the first topic, if you think about it just every company essentially goes through this kind of S-curve of growth. They start slow, they find something that's working, then hopefully it works out and things start to grow, grow, grow, and then eventually it flattens out and you see this S-curve that happens. And every company is always trying to find the next S-curve to add this layer on the cake that keeps overall growth up while this first growth channel slows.
turns.zh: 好，太棒。第一个话题开始，如果你想想，基本上每家公司都经历这种增长的 S 曲线。他们起得慢，找到管用的东西，然后希望它能成、开始长长长，最后摊平，你就看到这个 S 曲线。每家公司都一直在找下一个 S 曲线，给蛋糕加一层，在第一个增长渠道放缓时让整体增长保持住。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so people are always looking for what's the next thing? "Oh man, Clubhouse is coming out. We should get on Clubhouse." "Oh, TikTok is so hot, we've got to run some TikTok ads." And there's always something new, like newsletter ads, I don't know, podcast ads, if that's new. And you have a really interesting framework for how to think about this and make decisions and experiment. So, I'd love to hear insights there.
turns.zh: 所以人们一直在找下一个是什么？「哦天，Clubhouse 出来了。我们该上 Clubhouse。」「哦 TikTok 这么火，我们得投点 TikTok 广告。」总有新东西，比如 Newsletter 广告、我不知道，播客广告，如果那算新。你对怎么想这事、做决定、做实验有个很有意思的框架。我很想听那边的洞察。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: So, the exploring emerging channels framework that I'll take, either my teams or companies that I'm advising through, has three core ingredients that I like to spend time with. So, the first is really understanding if there is an overlap between what the customers need is, what your company's goals are, and what the channel actually does really well. So, the example I've used in the past is Spotify in the moment of things like Clubhouse and Paparazzi and stuff like that becoming really popular.
turns.zh: 我带团队或顾问公司时用的「探索新兴渠道框架」，有三个核心要素我想花时间。第一是真正理解：客户的需求、公司的目标、和这个渠道真正擅长的之间，有没有重叠。我过去用的例子是 Spotify，在 Clubhouse 和 Paparazzi 之类变得很火的时候。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Well, for Spotify, they're trying to get more people to consume music and be entertained by music and things like that. And it's all audio driven. And so their growth goals are probably around new customers or deeper engagement with audio. The customer's needs are discovery and more ways to maybe have deeper relationships with their music. If you're a jazz fan, can you learn new jazz artists or more about the artists that you love? Things like that. And then take those two channels. If you take something like Clubhouse, it's audio first, it's almost like live podcast radio type feel to it.
turns.zh: 对 Spotify，他们想让更多人消费音乐、被音乐娱乐之类。而且全是音频驱动。所以他们的增长目标大概是新客户、或者跟音频更深的互动。客户的需求是发现、以及更多方式也许跟他们的音乐建立更深的关系。如果你是爵士粉，你能不能学到新爵士艺术家、或者更多你爱的艺术家的事？诸如此类。然后拿这两个看渠道。如果你拿 Clubhouse，它是音频优先，几乎像直播播客电台的感觉。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: You can get into these rooms with just people with really amazing esoteric knowledge about something. And so its strengths have a really clean overlap to me with the goals of Spotify, the needs of the customer and the strengths of that. And so that to me is great. That is probably a green light in terms of is it even worth our time? Versus Paparazzi is very photo driven and nothing really to do with music or anything like that. And so it's like even though Paparazzi might have become the best biggest channel ever, is that the thing you should be putting your time into? It would be a yellow light for me at best.
turns.zh: 你能进这些房间，跟有某种超冷门知识的人一起。所以它的优势对我而言跟 Spotify 的目标、客户的需求、和那个渠道的优势，有很干净的重叠。所以对我来说是绿灯——值得花时间吗？而 Paparazzi 是照片驱动的，跟音乐之类的没什么关系。所以就算 Paparazzi 成了有史以来最大最好的渠道，那是你该投入时间的东西吗？对我来说最多是黄灯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And how did you describe that again? It's the medium matches?
turns.zh: 你刚怎么描述那个的？是媒介匹配？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Yeah, the strengths of the medium. So, let's take influencer right now. Actually two of the channels that a lot of people are talking about right now are streaming TV or OTT and influencer marketing. And so to me, one of the strengths of influencer marketing is hyper targeted contextual marketing. And so I can go find the five influencers that are hardcore Alf fans, and if I'm marketing Alf something, great, I can go find that specific thing. Whereas OTTs a lot harder to get that specific.
turns.zh: 对，媒介的优势。就拿 influencer（网红）现在说。其实大家现在聊得最多的两个渠道是流媒体电视（OTT）和网红营销。对我而言，网红营销的一个优势是超精准的情境营销。所以我可以找到五个硬核 Alf 粉的网红，如果我在营销 Alf 相关的东西，太好了，我能找到那个具体的东西。而 OTT 要那么具体就难多了。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: OTT strength is broad reach and video storytelling and that type of stuff. So, it's like, okay, well maybe my medium is if I'm Masterclass and I have a ton of video content and storytelling and things like that, that channel actually makes a ton of sense probably. So, it's like what are the strengths of that channel is something that... that is actually probably the piece I see people ignore the most, which is they just want to know if a channel is hot or not. And this gets especially hairy in this world of a lot of B2B doing more consumer-esque marketing. There's so many B2B companies that just don't apply to emerging consumer channels.
turns.zh: OTT 的优势是广覆盖和视频叙事之类。所以，如果你是我、是 MasterClass、有一堆视频内容和叙事，那个渠道其实可能非常说得通。所以，那个渠道的优势是什么——其实是我看到人们忽略最多的一块，他们只想知道一个渠道火不火。而这在一个很多 B2B 做更偏消费者的营销的世界里，变得特别棘手。太多 B2B 公司根本不适合新兴的消费者渠道。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: And it's just like, please just stop. I don't need a Notion Clubhouse channel this week. And maybe there's a world to do that. But I think that's kind of number one, is making sure that there's even a reason that you should be there to put it on your radar right now.
turns.zh: 就像，求求你停。我这周不需要一个 Notion Clubhouse 渠道。也许有世界能做那个。但我觉得第一点就是，确保甚至有个理由你该在那、把它放上你的雷达，现在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. What does the OTT stand for by the way?
turns.zh: 太棒了。顺便 OTT 代表什么？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Oh my gosh, you're putting it on the spot.
turns.zh: 哦天，你这是考我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's all good.
turns.zh: 没事。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: I'm drawing a blank on it.
turns.zh: 我一下想不起来了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But essentially it's a streaming platform?
turns.zh: 但 basically 是个流媒体平台？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Over the top. Over the top. So, instead of it being cable TV, it's coming from a box. So, it's primarily if you think of ads on Amazon or Hulu or even if you go to cnn.com and you start streaming and you get an ad first. it's basically video ads, but a lot of them now are happening on televisions and on streaming services rather than just on websites.
turns.zh: Over the top（OTT）。Over the top。所以不是有线电视，是来自一个盒子。所以主要是，如果你想 Amazon 或 Hulu 上的广告，或者你去 cnn.com 开始流、先来个广告。基本就是视频广告，但现在很多发生在电视和流媒体服务上，而不是只在网站上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay, cool. So, the first is the strength of the channel. You should look at that.
turns.zh: 懂了。好，酷。所以第一是渠道的优势。你该看那个。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Yep. And how that overlaps with your customer and your business needs. The second is the channel DNA. And so this is looking at things like where are they in their trajectory? So, Clubhouse is actually a perfect example, because in a weird way, so Clubhouse got hot before Facebook got cold. And I was pretty amazed how many more people were trying to crack Clubhouse than TikTok, because TikTok hadn't really released their ads solution yet, but neither had Clubhouse. But everybody was talking about Clubhouse, and TikTok is very clearly not going away anytime soon, where Clubhouse hopefully won't. Like this is an amazing product.
turns.zh: 对。以及它怎么跟你的客户和生意需求重叠。第二是渠道的 DNA。这是看它们在轨迹的哪。Clubhouse 其实是个完美的例子，因为很诡异地，Clubhouse 在 Facebook 变冷之前就火了。我挺惊讶有那么多人想攻克 Clubhouse 而不是 TikTok，因为 TikTok 还没真的放出他们的广告方案，但 Clubhouse 也没。但大家都在聊 Clubhouse，而 TikTok 很明显短期内不会消失，Clubhouse 希望也不会。就像这是个超棒的产品。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: I really enjoyed it and loved it, but it was clearly very early, very quickly at that point of hotness where everyone was just kind of, "That's the reason I should be there." And part of this reason is to accept the risks of going into that channel. So, if I go and dedicate two quarters of work to Clubhouse, I need to accept that they are so early in this curve that there's a good chance this is a once in a lifetime opportunity and it'll be over. It's not a repeatable action. It also is important because if you get something to work on a channel that's earlier in their growth curve, the likelihood that they will change is very high.
turns.zh: 我真的很享受、很爱它，但它明显非常早期，在那种「大家都『这就是我该在那的理由』」的热度点上非常快。这部分理由是要接受进那个渠道的风险。所以如果我投入两个季度的精力给 Clubhouse，我得接受他们在曲线上这么早，很可能有一次性的机会、然后就结束了。它不是可重复的动作。这也重要，因为如果你在一个增长曲线更早的渠道上做出点东西，他们改变的可能性非常高。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: You're going to need to commit a lot of cycles to keep it going, because it's like, "Okay, well, their product is going to evolve drastically very quickly over the next two years." And so a really great example is Facebook early... I was at Zoosk. And so Zoozk and companies like Zynga got tons of their early growth because of notifications on Facebook, which was one of their early features, which allowed basically anybody that took any action on Zynga, it would post on everybody else's page that you got 10 carrots, and that was a huge growth lever.
turns.zh: 你得投入很多周期去维持它，因为就像「好，他们的产品未来两年会飞速演变」。所以一个很好的例子是 Facebook 早期……我当时在 Zoosk。Zoosk 和 Zynga 这类公司早期的大量增长，来自 Facebook 的通知功能——那是他们早期的功能之一，基本是任何人在 Zynga 上做任何动作，都会在别人页面上发「你拿到了 10 个胡萝卜」，那是个巨大的增长杠杆。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: But then Facebook just pulled the plug on that. And so it's like, well, if you put all of your energy into that and that's it, it was pretty clear that that was still an area that's like this may not last forever. The last thing on the channel DNA that I like to look at that's a little bit more, I don't know if odd or unusual is the right term, is I like to spend a lot of time thinking about how they monetize. What is the monetization strategy of the channel? And the reason is because if you, as a business, can match or support their monetization strategy, it actually gives you a really interesting leg up with that channel.
turns.zh: 但后来 Facebook 直接把那个拔了。所以就像，如果你把所有精力都投在那、而且只投在那，那很明显那还是个「可能撑不了一辈子」的领域。渠道 DNA 上最后一点我想看的，有点，我不知道「奇怪」或「不寻常」对不对，是我喜欢花很多时间想他们怎么变现。渠道的变现策略是什么？原因是，如果你作为一家企业，能匹配或支持他们的变现策略，它其实给你在这个渠道上一个很有意思的先发优势。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Because the likelihood of you being able to call them up and go do custom stuff with them, or partner with them, or that your solutions will actually stick around for a while, it'd go up pretty drastically. And so my key example of this was with when Facebook started exploring mobile ads, Hotel Tonight, we were one of the alpha testers of mobile ads, because I'd been sitting here buying ad inventory on networks for the last five or six years and just waiting for Facebook to work, because it just wasn't really working for mobile installs.
turns.zh: 因为你能否打电话给他们、跟他们做定制的东西、或者合作、或者你的方案能真正留存一阵，概率会大幅提升。我这个的关键例子是 Facebook 开始探索移动广告时，Hotel Tonight——我们是移动广告的 alpha 测试者之一，因为我过去五六年一直在这买广告库存、就等着 Facebook 起作用，因为它对移动安装确实不怎么管用。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: And it's like, I know this is a huge channel because I can use it on my online marketing, my web marketing, but as a mobile acquisition it's nowhere near as efficient as a lot of these other networks. And so as soon as they were doing that, I was able to basically position and say, "Look it, you want to work with us. Let me into your alpha, because I have five years of experience already buying mobile ads. I know the space. I know it'll work. And if you get us to work, we're a killer case study, because we are a non-game and a lot of money is spent on gaming, but there's these whole other major categories that you're going to need other than gaming examples within that group. So, you're going to be able to use me as a case study and a lot of different scenarios than the gaming players."
turns.zh: 就像，我知道这是个巨大的渠道，因为我能用它在线上营销、网页营销，但作为移动获客，它远没有那些其他网络高效。所以一旦他们开始做那个，我基本就能定位、说「听着，你想跟我们合作。让我进你的 alpha，因为我已经有五年买移动广告的经验。我懂这块。我知道它会成。而且如果你让我们跑通，我们是个杀手级的案例研究，因为我们不是游戏，而很多钱花在游戏上，但除了游戏例子，那组里还有这些完全不同的大类你需要。所以你能用我当案例研究，在比游戏玩家多得多的场景里。」

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: And so I was spending a lot less than the gaming players, but because of that understanding that your goal at Facebook is to make ads work for all of travel and for all of leisure and those kinds of things, that's the value of working with me. So, that's another piece of the channel DNA I like people to focus on.
turns.zh: 所以我花的钱比游戏玩家少得多，但因为理解你在 Facebook 的目标是让广告对所有的旅游、所有的休闲之类都管用，那才是跟我们合作的价值。所以，这是渠道 DNA 里另一块我想让大家聚焦的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That's such a good one, because to your point, if your goals are aligned, they're going to be like, "Yes, let's make this happen." And it always feels like it's this behemoth that doesn't want to talk to any new startups, but if you can make the case of this is going to help you and the way you laid out is so clear, it's such a good idea.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这点真好，因为如你所说，如果目标一致，他们会「对，让这事成」。而且总觉得这是个不想跟任何新创业公司说话的巨兽，但如果你能讲出「这会帮到你」、而且你铺开的方式这么清楚，就是个好主意。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: And especially with emerging channels, right? Because their whole thing is that make this work for a long time. It's part of the challenge you see with some new channels flipping to the other side of growing an ads business, will gravitate towards like, "I want to get Disney on here," but Disney is very campaign driven, or they have been traditionally, where it's like you may get one big paycheck from them, but that doesn't... The way that UA driven gaming works is you get that to work, that's a gift that keeps on giving forever, right? Because there's not one of those companies, there's thousands of them and they all do the same thing. So, being able to drive that conversation is really helpful.
turns.zh: 尤其对新兴渠道，对吧？因为他们整件事就是要让这事长期管用。这是你看到一些新渠道翻到「做广告生意」那一面时的挑战之一——他们会倾向「我想把 Disney 弄上来」，但 Disney 是很活动驱动的，或者传统上如此，就像你可能从他们那拿到一张大支票，但那不……UA 驱动的游戏的玩法是你让它跑通，那是会永远给的礼物，对吧？因为那类公司不是一个，是几千个，他们都做一样的事。所以能驱动那场对话真的很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 酷。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: And then the third main ingredient is just your own company DNA. And so I think risk profile is a big one. Do you actually have comfort in being a first mover, a true first mover? Nobody knows anything, tracking's not going to work, it's not going to be programmatic. You're probably going to show up on content that's offensive. You're probably going to ask for refunds that won't happen. It's going to be really painful to be a true first mover. Do you have that appetite? Do you have the staff to actually be able to put someone on that and it not distract from everything else?
turns.zh: 然后第三个主要要素就是你自己的公司 DNA。我觉得风险偏好是大的一块。你真的舒服做第一个动的人、真正的先行者吗？没人知道任何事，追踪不会管用，不会是程序化的。你大概会出现在冒犯性的内容上。你大概会要求退款、但不会发生。做真正的先行者会非常痛苦。你有那个胃口吗？你有能放一个人上去、又不会分心所有别的事的人手吗？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: And then the other piece on the company side is just your current channel mix. There's very few companies that I recommend saying, "Yes, go put energy on this brand new channel that you don't know how to scale yet before you've figured out some type of volume on Google and Facebook." Every now and then there may be a perfect fit where it's like, absolutely, you should be the person doing this. But if you're not at least getting something out of the basic channels that everybody else is using, it's probably not the thing you should be putting your first energy into. It should be like, "Great, I've got a good foundation." Like you said, now we're at that stage of trying to add things, tends to be a better stage to do more risky exploration into new channels.
turns.zh: 然后公司这边的另一块就是你当前的渠道组合。我很少建议哪家公司说「对，在你还不知道怎么在 Google 和 Facebook 上跑出量之前，去把精力投在这个你还不知道怎么规模化的全新渠道上」。偶尔可能有完美匹配，就像，绝对，你该是做这个的人。但如果你连别人都在用的最基础渠道都还没跑出点东西，那大概不是你该投第一份精力的地方。应该是像「好，我有了不错的基础。」就像你说的，现在我们在那个想加东西的阶段，往往是做更冒险的新渠道探索的更好阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What advice do you have or can you give to founders teams that are trying to test one of these in terms of just how to run these tests? How much time should they spend, would you say? What do they look for? I know that this is a hard question and super dependent on the situation, but any advice there?
turns.zh: 你有什么建议给那些想测其中一个的创始人团队，关于怎么跑这些测试？你觉得他们该花多少时间？他们看什么？我知道这是个难的问题、非常看情况，但那边有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: So, I think going through those three ingredients should help shape that answer, right? Because if you're like, "Okay, well, the first one is super strong, the channel DNA is maybe really early and I've got a small to mid-size team and maybe only one channel working," then it may be like, "Great. Put half of one person into this, because it's maybe interesting. But don't put any more than that into it." Versus if it's like, "Man, this is a killer fit the channel's a little further along and I have a 20 person team, so I'm going to put three dedicated people to this, because we are in prime position to be the leaders in this new channel and really push it."
turns.zh: 所以，我觉得过完那三个要素应该能帮着塑造那个答案，对吧？因为如果你像「好，第一个超强，渠道 DNA 可能真的很早期、我有个中小团队、可能只有一个渠道在跑」，那可能像「好。放半个人进去，因为可能有点意思。但别投更多了。」而如果是「天，这是个绝配、渠道再往前走一点、我有 20 人团队，所以我要放三个专职人进去，因为我们正处于能当这个新渠道领导者、真正推它的位置。」

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: So, I think it's figuring those pieces out, because it is a very it depends answer, but rarely ever is it like, "Hey, this should be your entire team's focus for the next three sprints or five sprints." I think that if you've got that half person working on it for a while and there starts to be some magic happening, sure, put a sprint or two against it as a whole team. But generally speaking, I think keeping it minimum at first is my typical recommendation.
turns.zh: 所以，我觉得是搞清楚那些块，因为它真的是个「看情况」的答案，但很少是「嘿，这该是你整个团队接下来三个或五个 sprint 的焦点」。我觉得如果那半个人干了一阵、开始有点 magic 发生，当然，作为整个团队投一两个 sprint。但 generally 来说，我觉得一开始保持最小是我典型的建议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I had another guest, Yuri, who I think from former Grammarly, and he made a really good point that it's often better not to try something than to do it badly and then take away the wrong lessons. I guess, in your experience, what's a timeframe you think people should put into this stuff? You said two sprints, maybe a couple weeks. I don't know, what's the range of just maybe don't spend more than X months on something new if it's not clearly working, just based on your experience.
turns.zh: 我另一个嘉宾 Yuri，我想是前 Grammarly 的，他提了个很好的点：往往不试，比做得很烂然后得出错误教训要好。我想，按你的经验，你觉得人们该投多少时间到这种事上？你说两个 sprint，也许几周。我不知道，基于你的经验，大概就是如果明显不 work，别在一样新东西上花超过 X 个月？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Generally I wouldn't let anything bleed past a quarter. You can probably get some good signal in a month or less, what I would call fishing. It wouldn't be like you're just putting bait in the water to figure out where the fish are, not necessarily getting statistically significant repeatable solutions. The big variables that can change that timing, so if I'm exploring a new video channel, the content I need to create is if I'm going to have to create something that takes three weeks to produce and $20,000 to make, I may want to give it a little more time, because I gave it more of an upfront investment.
turns.zh: Generally 我不会让任何事拖过一个季度。你可能一个月甚至更短就能拿到些好信号，我所谓的「钓鱼」。不是你只是把饵放进水里弄清鱼在哪，不一定是拿到统计显著、可重复的方案。能改变那个时机的大的变量：如果我在探索一个新的视频渠道，我需要做的内容如果要花三周制作、两万美元做，我可能想多给点时间，因为我 upfront 投入更多。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Versus if it's like I want to put text ads in podcasts listings or something like that. It's like, great, I can do that by myself at midnight and it's not distracting anybody or anything. And if it doesn't work in three weeks, let's move on. But generally ideally what you're working through, and we'll touch a little bit more on this with the Growth CMO, is that this should all be part of a roadmap. It shouldn't just be randomly chosen and thrown at. This should be part of your sprint process and you should have a backlog of other things that you want to try. And so you're actually weighing that decision of how long based on what other opportunities you're missing out on by investing in that.
turns.zh: 而如果是我想在播客列表里放文字广告之类，就像，好，我半夜自己就能做、不分心任何人任何事。如果三周不 work，就撤。但 generally 理想的是你在过的，我们聊增长型 CMO 会再碰一点，就是这都该是一个路线图的一部分。不该是随机选了就扔上去。这该是你 sprint 流程的一部分，你该有个想试的其他东西的 backlog。所以你其实是在权衡那个决定——投这个，你错过了别的什么机会。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: But I would say most channels, especially new ones, are going to take more than a couple cycles to kind of suss out. Because there's no rules, there's no playbooks yet on how to do them well. So, give it a little bit of time, but if you're going over a quarter and you don't feel like directionally it's getting better or it's interesting, I would put it back on ice for a while.
turns.zh: 但我会说多数渠道，尤其新的，要花不止几个周期才能摸清。因为没规则，还没怎么做才好的 playbook。所以给点时间，但如果你超过一个季度、而且方向感上不觉得在变好或有趣，我会把它放回冰柜一阵。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. And to your point, you're not going to see any statistically significant answers. Is the thing you look for just like you know it when you see it? Oh wow, qualitatively feels like it's working kind of thing? Is that what you kind of look for?
turns.zh: 酷。如你所说，你不会看到任何统计显著的答案。你看的东西就是「看到了就知道」？哦哇，定性上感觉它在 work 那种？那是你大概看的吗？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Yeah, and I think define that going into it. What am I looking for, for this? So, something like Clubhouse I'm probably not going to see clicks. It's more about are we able to start a room and increase the size of that room by 10% every time that we run it? Okay great, that means that we're at least getting better at this and there's more reach available to us. But if we're getting 20 people every time we start a room and then it goes down to 15, then we're either not doing this well, the channel's not doing well, or there's just not enough reach for us to actually expand. Versus TikTok you might be able to say, "Great, I can actually track clicks and conversion, so let's look at it the way we would any other channel."
turns.zh: 对，而且我觉得进去之前就定义那个。我为这个在找什么？所以像 Clubhouse，我大概不会看到点击。更多是「我们能不能开个房间、每次跑的时候把房间大小涨 10%？」好，那就意味着我们至少在这变好、有更大的触达可用。但如果我们每次开房间都是 20 人、然后掉到 15，那要么是我们没做好、渠道没做好、要么就是没足够触达让我们真扩。而 TikTok 你可能能说「好，我能真的追踪点击和转化，所以像别的渠道一样看它。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So, kind of look for momentum and that you're getting better and that it's moving somewhere. Awesome.
turns.zh: 懂了。所以就是看动量、你在变好、它在往哪动。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Yeah. Yep.
turns.zh: 对。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. So, a question that I'm sure is on many people's minds that they would want to ask is, Adam, what are emerging platforms that are interesting right now that we should experiment with? What do you feel?
turns.zh: 酷。所以一个我肯定很多人心里想问的问题是，Adam，现在有什么有意思的、我们该去试的新兴平台？你怎么感觉？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: So, I mean I mentioned OTT, or basically the key thing with OTT is that it's way more trackable than traditional television, but it has similar value that traditional TV does in terms of the ability to do more long form storytelling type content, and a lot of it's not skippable if you buy it. And so those are reasons to be exploring that right now. It's hard for me to call that emerging channel, because it's been around forever. It's there's more of it and the tools and services around it are way better now than they were four years ago. And so I think the sophistication and ability to scale OTT is much higher now than ever before. Influencers probably the one that I'm most intrigued by, because similar to OTT, the scale and services and the ability to go do it is still there.
turns.zh: 我提到了 OTT，或者 basically OTT 的关键是它比传统电视可追踪得多，但有传统电视类似的价值——能做更长形式的叙事类内容，而且很多你买了就不可跳过。所以那些是现在去探索它的理由。我很难叫它新兴渠道，因为它一直都在。只是现在更多了，围绕它的工具和服务比四年前好太多。所以我觉得 OTT 的成熟度和规模化能力现在比以前高得多。网红可能是我最被勾起兴趣的，因为跟 OTT 类似，规模、服务和去做的能力都还在。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: It's also got that hyper granularity that when I get into influencer tools, it feels to me like early Facebook when I used to go be able to target Lenny, or 10 people that have exactly the same likes as Lenny. And that type of stuff where it's like you can get so specific and find exactly who you need. It's incredibly tedious and manual and it's a lot of relationship management. So, I'm also keeping an eye on the technology being built around influencer, because I think that's a huge area of opportunity for entrepreneurs right now.
turns.zh: 它还有那种超细颗粒度，当我进网红工具时，对我而言像早期 Facebook——那时我能去定向 Lenny、或者 10 个跟 Lenny 一模一样喜好的人。那种你能这么具体、精确找到你需要的人。它极度繁琐、手工，而且很多关系管理。所以我也在盯着围绕网红在建的技术，因为我觉得那是现在创业者一个巨大的机会领域。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: But generally speaking, the scope and opportunity there is huge and it's not going away, but it feels very new and different right now. And it supplements the ability to do some hyper level targeting that you've not been able to do, that Facebook and Google are getting less open about at the same time. I think VR is really interesting in the way that mobile was interesting before iPhone Three, where it was if you've got a VR app, it's a really interesting space, but if you don't, it's not that interesting to me yet. Any that have come up for you that you're like... what are your thoughts on this?
turns.zh: 但 generally 来说，那边的范围和机会巨大、而且不会消失，但现在感觉很新、很不一样。而且它补充了做某种超层级定向的能力——你以前做不到，而 Facebook 和 Google 同时在这块越来越不开放。我觉得 VR 很有意思，就像 iPhone 3 之前移动很有意思那样——如果你有个 VR app，那是个很有意思的空间，但如果你没有，它还不太让我感兴趣。有什么冒出来让你觉得……你怎么看这个？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, these are great. All I think of is TikTok.
turns.zh: 不，这些都很好。我只想到 TikTok。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: I feel like TikTok's crossed a chasm, whereas they actually have a formalized ad platform now, people are finding scale. There's still a ton to do there and influencers is also weird, because it crosses all of these other worlds as well. But I think TikTok is actually hyper interesting and everyone should be doing that. But I think of that less as you should be doing it as should I do it, should I not? And it's more I need to figure out how to do Facebook if I'm at least mildly appropriately should be there.
turns.zh: 我觉得 TikTok 已经跨过鸿沟了，因为他们现在真有个成形的广告平台，人们在找到规模。那边还有一大堆可做，而且网红也很诡异，因为它也跨所有这些别的世界。但我觉得 TikTok 其实超有意思、每个人该做。但我更少想成「你该不该做」，更多是「如果我在那至少适度合适，我需要想清楚怎么像做 Facebook 那样去做。」

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: The podcast ads I think are great. I think that I bought podcast ads 15 years ago, so it doesn't feel like an emerging channel to me. I think there's way more volume now than there's ever been before. One of the guys that was on my team at Uber has a company that's doing programmatic buying and that type of stuff. And so I think there's more opportunities on podcast. I think people want to treat it like Facebook ads or direct response ads, immediate response ads. And actually what I keep seeing as the effective strategy with podcast ads is treating them more like radio where it's more about getting on the right program, making it personal and feel like it should be part of that program, and then repeating over and over and over again.
turns.zh: 播客广告我觉得很好。我 15 年前就买过播客广告，所以对我而言它不感觉像新兴渠道。我觉得现在的量比以往任何时候都大。我 Uber 团队里的一个哥们有个公司在做程序化购买之类。所以我觉得播客上机会更多。人们想把它当 Facebook 广告或直效广告、即时响应广告对待。而其实我一直看到的播客广告有效策略，是更像电台——更多是上对的节目、让它个人化、感觉它该是那个节目的一部分，然后一遍一遍又一遍地重复。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: So, I think podcast is super interesting. I think it's just hard to scale. It's likely not going to get people the same volumes as the Googles and Facebooks of the world.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得播客超有意思。我只是觉得难规模化。它可能不会给人 Google 和 Facebook 那种量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cue our mid-roll ad. I'm excited to chat with my friend John Cutler from Podcast sponsor, Amplitude. Hey John.
turns.zh: cue 我们的 mid-roll 广告。我很兴奋跟我的朋友、播客赞助商 Amplitude 的 John Cutler 聊。嘿 John。

turns.speaker: John Cutler
turns.en: Hey, Lenny. Excited to be here.
turns.zh: 嘿 Lenny。很高兴来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: John, give us a behind the scenes at Amplitude. When most people think of Amplitude, they think of product analytics, but now you're getting into experimentation and even just launched a CDP. What's the thought process there?
turns.zh: John，给我们讲讲 Amplitude 幕后。大多数人想到 Amplitude 想到产品分析，但现在你们在做实验、甚至刚发了个 CDP。那边的思路是什么？

turns.speaker: John Cutler
turns.en: Well, we've always thought of Amplitude as being about supporting the full product loop. Think collect data, inform bets, ship experiments and learn. That's the heart of growth to us. So, the big aha was seen how many customers were using Amplitude to analyze experiments, use segments for outreach and send data to other destinations. Experiment and CDP came out of listening to and observing our customers.
turns.zh: 我们一直把 Amplitude 想成支持完整的产品闭环。想想：收数据、inform 下注、发实验、学。那是我们增长的核心。所以那个大 aha 是看到多少客户在用 Amplitude 分析实验、用分群做触达、把数据发到别的地方。实验和 CDP 来自倾听和观察我们的客户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And supporting growth and learning has always been Amplitude's core focus, right?
turns.zh: 而且支持增长和学习一直是 Amplitude 的核心焦点，对吧？

turns.speaker: John Cutler
turns.en: Yeah. So, Amplitude tries to meet customers where they are. We just launched starter templates and have a great scholarship program for startups. There's never been a more important time for growth.
turns.zh: 对。所以 Amplitude 尽量在客户所在的地方接住他们。我们刚发了 starter 模板，还有个给初创公司的奖学金项目。从来没比现在更适合增长的时候了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely agree. Thanks for joining us, John, and head to amplitude.com to get started.
turns.zh: 完全同意。谢谢你来，John，去 amplitude.com 开始吧。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: I also come from a very consumer perspective. I'm actually stronger on B2B companies using podcasting, because it has that exact same value I just described, but each one of their customers is substantially more valuable. So, they don't need the scale that a consumer application or product would need.
turns.zh: 我也来自一个非常消费者的视角。其实我在 B2B 公司用播客上更强，因为它有我刚描述的完全相同的价值，但他们每个客户的价值都大得多。所以他们不需要消费者应用或产品需要的那种规模。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yep. That's exactly who I work with usually. One last question on this topic. What percentage of the time do you find that an emerging channel works? Is it like 20% of the time, 10%, 5%? What should people estimate, it's probably not going to work but when it does it's going to be game changing?
turns.zh: 对。那基本就是我通常合作的对象。这个话题最后一个问题。你发现一个新兴渠道 work 的百分比是多少？是像 20%、10%、5%？人们该估计多少——大概不会 work，但 work 了就是改变游戏规则？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Like 5% of the time. There's new things popping up all the time. I think the area that I think of as emerging that I've found more success in is taking things that exist already and make them... so the two slices of it are either it's existed for a long... like podcasting. So, it existed for a long time and now we're finally getting to a spot where it feels scalable. The other is existing channels that introduce something brand new.
turns.zh: 大概 5% 的时间。新东西一直在冒。我觉得我所谓的「新兴」、而且找到更多成功的，是拿已经存在的东西、让它们……所以两片：要么是存在很久的……比如播客。所以它存在很久、现在我们终于到一个感觉可规模化的点。另一片是引入全新东西的现有渠道。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: So, at the mobile ads I described on Facebook, pre mobile install ads and post. Those first 18 months of mobile install felt like an emerging channel, right? Because they were changing the product every week and tracking didn't work, and there were all these funky problems with it even though Facebook had been around forever. But brand spanking new channels, I don't know, they rarely work or are worth the effort early that you hope that they will be.
turns.zh: 所以，我描述的 Facebook 移动广告，在移动安装广告之前和之后。那头 18 个月的移动安装感觉像个新兴渠道，对吧？因为他们每周改产品、追踪不 work，还有各种诡异问题，尽管 Facebook 一直都在。但全新渠道，我不知道，早期很少 work、或者值得你希望投的精力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. But when they work, it's game changing I imagine. Reminds me Apples coming out with Apple TV, I think it was, and they're just like, "Hey Airbnb, you should make it app for Apple TV. It'll be huge." And there's a team put on it. I don't know. They spent a month building this app and did a bunch of nothing as far as I understand, but it felt good. It felt good to be part of the launch. One question I wanted to come back to, are there tools that you recommend for influencer marketing that you want to plug, or point out?
turns.zh: 酷。但 work 了，我猜就是改变游戏规则。让我想起 Apple 出 Apple TV，我想是，他们就「嘿 Airbnb，你该给 Apple TV 做个 app。会很大。」然后放了支团队。我不知道。他们花了一个月建这个 app，据我所知啥也没做成，但感觉好。成为发布一部分感觉好。我想回到一个问题，有没有你推荐的网红营销工具想 plug 或指出的？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: We were using Grin at Masterclass, we onboarded them. So, there's probably half a dozen companies in that same zone where they're building tools that allow you to do the discovery of influencers, the CRM of those influencers, and also often the measurement and payments and all that kind of stuff. So, it's an all in one type of management platform. That being said though, like I said, it's still super manual. It's nice to be able to go and find this list of 50 influencers that are the exact right influencer for this class launch, or whatever it might be.
turns.zh: 我们在 MasterClass 用 Grin，我们 onboard 了他们。所以那同一个区里大概有半打公司在建工具，让你做网红的发现、那些网红的 CRM，而且常常还有测量和支付所有那些。所以是个一体化管理平台。话虽如此，就像我说，它还是很手工。能去找到这 50 个网红的清单、正好是这堂发布对的网红，或者不管什么，是挺好。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: But it's still then I have to wait till they all respond to me and there's still a lot of manual back and forth. So, that's probably one of them. I'm trying to think of... There's a few other in that same category that are competitive with Grin that they all seem equally pretty good. I can't even remember the reason we chose Grin over some of the other ones.
turns.zh: 但还是然后我得等他们全回我、还有很多手工来回。所以那大概是其中一个。我在想……同品类里还有几个跟 Grin 竞争的，看起来都差不多好。我甚至不记得我们选 Grin 而不是别的一些的理由。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a good name.
turns.zh: 名字好。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: It was all pretty close.
turns.zh: 都挺接近的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. Okay. If any other comes to mind, we'll throw it in the show notes. Before we get to the growth CMO discussion, there's kind of this tangential area that I wanted to spend a little time on, which is this idea of as a startup you initially should and often do start with a very narrow audience, your early adopters. I read this post about calling them your super specific who, and eventually you want to cross the chasm and go broader. And you have some interesting insights on how to think about that, and when to do that. Can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 甜。好。如果还想到别的，我们放进节目笔记。在进增长型 CMO 讨论前，有个我想花点时间的旁支领域，就是作为初创公司，你最初应该、也常常确实从一个非常窄的受众、你的早期采用者开始。我读到一篇帖子把叫他们你「超具体的谁」，最终你想跨过鸿沟、走得更宽。你对怎么想这个、什么时候做，有些有意思的洞察。能讲讲吗？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Yeah. So, I think the book, Crossing the Chasm, is a great place to start in terms of thinking about the broader topic of that. What I see missed a lot of the time that I like to spend time with people on is to really understand that those early adopters are often just drastically different than the broad audience. And spending time to actually figure that out and map out what you need to see with those early adopters to have confidence that the product is actually going to have product market fit beyond them.
turns.zh: 对。所以我觉得《跨越鸿沟》这本书是思考那个更宽话题的好起点。我看到常被漏掉、而我喜欢花时间跟人聊的，是真正理解那些早期采用者常常跟宽受众彻底不同。花时间真正搞清楚那个、并画出你需要从早期采用者身上看到什么，才能有信心产品真的会在他们之外有产品市场契合。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: So, I don't have anything hyper specific to add to that necessarily, or happy to dig in deeper to it, but it's probably the biggest challenge that I've seen with a lot of companies that I've worked with. And then as I do more investing and things like that, it's probably the biggest flag that I see with a lot of companies that claim to have product market fit, which is your TAM and your product market fit are not using the same definition. And that problem I think is often just a red flag for a lot of companies that I meet.
turns.zh: 所以我不一定有超具体的东西要加、或者乐意深挖，但那可能是我跟很多合作公司看到的最大挑战。而且随着我做更多投资之类，那可能是我看到很多声称有产品市场契合的公司最大的红旗——你的 TAM 和你的产品市场契合用的不是同一个定义。而那个问题我觉得常是很多我见过的公司的红旗。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So, essentially you often underestimate how challenging it'll be to grow from your initial early adopter crowd. Is there an example of that happening where a company just got screwed because they didn't think about that enough? Or is there something someone can do early on? Is it test a little bit more broadly early? What do you recommend there?
turns.zh: 懂了。所以 basically 你常低估从最初早期采用者人群长起来会有多难。有没有那种公司因为想得不够、然后被搞死的例子？或者早期有什么人能做的？是早点测广一点？你那边建议什么？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: I mean Clubhouse might be a good example in the sense that they leaned into the broader audience maybe quicker than they should have. Their product market fit seemed to fit the moment in time and could they have built some experiments, or tools, or features that maybe stress tested will this work in an ongoing fashion? If they were on such tear, that's a pretty hard decision to make, I'm sure.
turns.zh: 我是说 Clubhouse 可能是个好例子，在某种意义上他们比应该的更快靠向了宽受众。他们的产品市场契合似乎契合那个时点，而他们能不能建些实验、或工具、或功能来压力测试「这能持续 work 吗？」如果他们当时冲那么猛，那是个挺难的决定，我肯定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So hard, it's easy in hindsight.
turns.zh: 太难了，事后看容易。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: I think that's another piece of it is that the audience changes aren't always just literal people. Even right now, one of the biggest pieces of advice I'm giving to people that are like, "How should we adjust our marketing with the economic changes and things like that?" I was like, "Start by assuming you no longer have product market fit, because you had product market fit in a different market. It's a different market now, so you have to start over."
turns.zh: 我觉得那是另一块——受众的变化不总只是字面的人。即使现在，我给那些问「经济变化了，我们该怎么调整营销？」的人的最大一条建议是：「先假设你们已经没有产品市场契合了，因为你是在一个不同的市场里有的。现在市场不一样了，所以你得从头来。」

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: And hopefully you do, or it's pretty close to it and you just have to adjust a couple things and you can be right back on track. But if you just assume you need to launch a new channel to fix this problem, you're going to be wrong, because your entire customer base changed, not just the next 10% of customers that you're looking for.
turns.zh: 希望你是这样，或者离那很近、只要调几样就能重回正轨。但如果你只是假设你需要上线一个新渠道来修这个问题，那你就错了，因为你的整个客户群都变了，不只是你找的下一个 10% 的客户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's just a reminder of how freaking hard startups are. Man, we have product market fit. Okay, we're done. Let's move on.
turns.zh: 这只是提醒创业有多他妈难。哥们，我们有产品市场契合了。好，我们完了。继续。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Not anymore.
turns.zh: 不再有了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not anymore. Oh man. Okay, sweet. So, onto this next topic around the Growth CMO. So, you're this really interesting combination of marketing brain and also very analytical growth person, and I think you refer to this as Growth CMO, which I don't actually hear the term much. So, I'm curious, what is a Growth CMO? How do you define it? And why is it important?
turns.zh: 不再有了。哦哥们。好，甜。转到下一个话题：增长型 CMO。你是个很有意思的组合——营销脑加上也很分析的增长人，而且我想你管这叫增长型 CMO，我其实不常听到这个词。所以我好奇，什么是增长型 CMO？你怎么定义？为什么重要？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Yeah, so it's something I've just spent a lot of the last few years thinking about, specifically because now I've been at a handful of companies where we've brought in CMOs that in all ways are absolute world class CMOs, and they don't last, they don't fit and they don't succeed. And so I've spent a lot of time and figuring, well, why not? Some of it coming because of spending time with those people being like, "Why are you doing it this way? That's not how a company at our stage operates."
turns.zh: 对，这是我过去几年花很多时间想的，特别因为现在我在好几家公司，我们招了 CMO，从各方面都是世界级 CMO，但他们待不住、不合、不成功。所以我花很多时间搞清楚，为啥不？部分来自跟那些人待着，像「你为啥这么干？那不是我们这个阶段公司运作的方式。」

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Trying to do it the way that a traditional CMO would've done marketing for a company, et cetera. One of the key examples I like to use is brand, in that everybody when they think about brand they think of it as an action, not as a consistent ongoing investment, or they think about it as campaigns and things like that. And from planning to execution to learnings, a traditional CMO will drive learnings and identify learnings. And in my mind, I think a Growth CMO is looking at each brand investment as how do you then immediately follow that up with the next one? How do you shift to this fast product iteration mindset with even things like brand?
turns.zh: 试图用传统 CMO 会给公司做营销的方式做，等等。我喜欢用的一个关键例子是品牌——每个人想到品牌都把它当个动作，不是当持续的投入，或者他们想到的是活动之类。而从规划到执行到学习，传统 CMO 会驱动学习、识别学习。而在我脑子里，我觉得增长型 CMO 是把每个品牌投入都看成「然后你怎么立刻跟上下一个？」你怎么即使对品牌这类东西，也转到这种快速产品迭代的心态？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: It's very possible, but it's so counter to a lot of traditional marketing DNA. That, to me, means that we have a lot of mismatch marketing leadership, and that quickly eliminates trust with the marketing organization. It means that we rename everything marketing to product led growth, or growth, or referral programs. To me, it actually dilutes the value of marketing should be playing in the company. And it doesn't mean that the traditional marketing CMO isn't a good fit for some companies.
turns.zh: 这完全可能，但它跟很多传统营销 DNA 太反了。那对我而言，意味着我们有很多错配的营销领导，而那很快消磨掉对营销组织的信任。它意味着我们把所有营销改名成产品驱动增长、或增长、或推荐项目。对我而言，那其实稀释了营销本该在公司里扮演的价值。而且那不意味着传统营销 CMO 不适合某些公司。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: I think the direct to consumer products are still very well suited to have a more traditional CMO. But I think product driven companies, product led companies, if you are CMO and your product leader aren't married at the hip, you're just missing out on just tons of opportunity, and the likelihood of things actually working very well consistently and compounding on each other.
turns.zh: 我觉得 direct to consumer 产品还是非常适合有个更传统的 CMO。但我觉得产品驱动的公司、产品 led 的公司，如果你是个 CMO、而你的产品领导不跟你绑在 hip 上，你就错过了海量的机会，以及事情真的持续很好 work、互相复利的可能性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, what are the attributes of this person of what you call a Growth CMO? Sounds like partly it's being much more performance driven. Sounds like a big part of it is understanding product and not creating these silos. We're going to market the thing, you guys go build this thing. But also as a person, that's a great CMO. What else do you look for?
turns.zh: 所以，这个人的属性，你叫增长型 CMO 的，是什么？听起来部分是非常更绩效驱动。听起来很大一块是懂产品、不造这些筒仓。我们要去市场那个东西，你们去建那个东西。但作为一个人，那是个好 CMO。你还看什么？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: So, I would say so data driven generally. To me performance is a very loaded word in our world, because people think, especially in marketing, think that means not brand. But they're very data driven. And so when we take things like retention and even brand and the consideration funnel and, yes, you can't measure those exactly like you can measure landing page clicks and sales, but you absolutely can measure them. And making that part of the DNA of everything that's happening, data being part of that, I think is pretty quintessential of being a growth driven CMO.
turns.zh: 所以我会说，总体是数据驱动。对我而言「绩效」在我们这行是个很有负担的词，因为人们、尤其营销里，觉得那意味不是品牌。但他们是非常数据驱动的。所以当我们拿留存、甚至品牌和考虑漏斗这种东西，对，你不能像量落地页点击和销量那样精确量它们，但你绝对能量。而且把它变成发生的一切的 DNA 的一部分、数据成为其中一部分，我觉得是增长驱动型 CMO 的典型特征。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: The second, I think, is the iteration process is not thinking about things and, "Hey, we need to plan for the next 24 months," but you can still do that and you can still have a vision and everything. But having that more of a agile type approach to everything. And again, this could be the storytelling that your sales people are doing, to what are your landing pages look like, to what is the design of your logo, to the brand itself. All of those things, like being more open to everything being possibly iterated on, on a regular basis using data to validate that and challenge what has worked for you.
turns.zh: 第二，我觉得是迭代过程——不是想「嘿，我们要为接下来 24 个月做计划」，但你还是能做那个、还是能有愿景和一切。而是对所有东西有更敏捷的方式。再说一遍，这可以是你销售在做的叙事、你的落地页长啥样、你的 logo 设计、品牌本身。所有这些，更敞开让一切都能定期被迭代，用数据去验证、去挑战对你管用的东西。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: We live in such a real time world now, especially with product driven companies. The things change so quickly. If you as a marketing leader aren't being iterative and thoughtful about things with it, you'll get eaten alive. And then I think experimentation is just a huge piece of it. And something that I see a lot of more traditional marketing leaders, the idea of experimentation is try a new channel. It's not like how do we experiment with our brand? How do we experiment with the funnel? The whole picture, not just the top of the funnel or the external elements of it.
turns.zh: 我们现在活在这么实时的世界，尤其产品驱动的公司。东西变得这么快。如果你作为营销领导不迭代、不深思，你会被生吞。然后我觉得实验只是巨大的一块。而我看到很多更传统的营销领导，实验的概念是「试个新渠道」。不是「我们怎么拿品牌做实验？我们怎么拿漏斗做实验？」整张图，不只是漏斗顶部或外部元素。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: One of the things that I haven't quite figured out the right language to put against this, but the traditional model of marketing is the four P's, product, placement, promotion, pricing. And in my mind, the world that we live in now, product is no longer a part of marketing, but it's actually they're married at the hip. They're one and the same, and most companies aren't operating that way. They're still operating as if they're two wildly different things. Even if they say they're working together, it's still, there's not. And to me it's just like, no, no, the product, it is the company now.
turns.zh: 有件事我还没想出正确的语言来表达，但传统营销模型是 4P——产品、渠道、促销、定价。而在我脑子里，我们现在活的世界，产品不再是营销的一部分，而是其实他们绑在 hip 上。它们是同一个。大多公司不是那么运作的。他们还在当这是两个截然不同的东西运作。即使说在一起工作，其实没有。而对我而言就是，不不，产品，它现在就是公司。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: And the marketing is integrated with literally every single piece of it. A lot of traditional marketing got established in the 1920s and the 1950s around products that took years to develop or try, or a product team was a science group trying new flavors of cereal. And so the marketing team owned the box, where it went on the shelf and what the price was and all of those kinds of things was marketing, because product was such a wildly different part of the organization. And I think still there's just a lot of fundamental things that marketers think about that are stuck in that world, because most haven't had to grow through the true growth of a business that's just being established today.
turns.zh: 而营销是跟它的每一块都整合的。很多传统营销在 1920 和 1950 年代建立，围绕那些要花几年开发或试的产品、或者产品团队是个科学组在试新麦片口味。所以营销团队拥有那个盒子、它放货架哪、价格多少、所有那些是营销，因为产品是组织里那么不同的部分。而我觉得还是有很多营销人想的底层东西卡在那个世界里，因为大多没经历过今天刚立起来的公司真正的增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the assumption is every software company should be hiring a CMO that is of this sort, of a Growth CMO, right?
turns.zh: 而假设是每家软件公司都该招这种 CMO，增长型 CMO，对吧？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Yeah. And I would say that my sense is that there's very few marketing leaders that can't be a Growth CMO. So, I don't think you have to have come up as a performance driven experimentation. It's more about adapting and growing. And again, the fundamentals are all the same. One of my pet projects that I haven't done anything with yet, is that every time something new comes out in the growth world, I go back in history as far as I can to try to find the earliest example of that. Just to be able to say, "Look, this isn't new, but we can learn from the way that Coca-Cola invented the coupon."
turns.zh: 对。我会说我的感觉是，很少营销领导不能成为增长型 CMO。所以我不觉得你得从绩效驱动的实验起来。更多是适应和成长。再说一遍，底层都一样。我有个还没动手的 pet project，是增长世界每次出新产品，我都尽量往历史回找最早的例子。就为了能说「看，这不新，但我们能从 Coca-Cola 发明优惠券的方式学」。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: The first known coupon was Coca-Cola giving away Coke for free, but it was actually a marketplace, because what they would do is they would go to a town and they would go to the soda fountain and they would give a free Coke syrup to that side of the market and they would give coupons to the other side of the market to spark it, to get it going. And then it's like, well, now all the customers want Coke, now you need to supply it, you'll pay for it. And learning that and understanding that is really cool. And it's just interesting to me, because I'm a huge nerd.
turns.zh: 已知第一张优惠券是 Coca-Cola 免费送可乐，但它其实是个市场——因为他们会去一个镇、去汽水喷泉，给那一侧市场免费可乐糖浆，给另一侧市场优惠券来点燃它、让它转起来。然后就像，好，现在所有客户都想要可乐，现在你需要供货，你会付钱。学到那个、理解那个真的酷。而它对我有意思，因为我是个大书呆子。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: But that to me is all of the things that great marketing leaders have learned are right, it's the operating aspect of those insights and those skills and understanding your customer and their psychology. All of those things have stayed the same. It's the operating of it in the way a growth organization, like a product driven growth organization operates, is very fundamentally different than the way a traditional marketing run organization had run.
turns.zh: 但那对我而言，是所有好营销领导学到的对的东西——是那些洞察和技能、理解你的客户和他们的心理的运作层面。所有那些都没变。变的是在增长组织、像产品驱动增长组织运作的方式里运作它，跟传统营销运作的组织运作方式非常根本地不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was going to ask you what a marketing leader can do to evolve into this where you think things are going, and your point about you're capable of it, you can iterate and adapt is really great and empowering. Is there anything specific they can do to learn how to do this better, other than is it like mentorship? Is there classes, courses? Just do the job, figure it out? Do you have anything you can suggest there to folks listening and they're like, "Oh, shit. I'm in trouble?"
turns.zh: 我正要问你，一个营销领导能做什么来演化成这个、你觉得到哪去，而你关于「你能做到、你能迭代适应」的点真的很好、很赋能。有没有具体他们能做的、去学怎么把这做得更好，还是像导师？有课、课程？就做这份工作、搞清楚？你有什么能建议给听的、然后「哦糟，我有麻烦了」的人？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Honestly, I think learn product development. Go learn agile product development. And there's actually a book called Hacking Marketing, I think. I'll confirm. But it's essentially how to run a marketing team on Agile. That to me is just, again, any great marketing leader should be able to go and consume how to do product development, how to run a product like sprints and those types of things. And their mind, if they're great marketing CMO or a CMO, will be like, "Oh my gosh, I could do this with this big event that we want to host. I could do this with everything."
turns.zh: 老实说，我觉得学产品开发。去学敏捷产品开发。有本叫《Hacking Marketing》的书，我想。我确认下。但它基本是怎么用敏捷跑营销团队。那对我而言就是，再说一遍，任何好营销领导都该能去消化怎么做产品开发、怎么用像 sprint 那样跑产品。他们的脑子，如果是好营销 CMO 或 CMO，会像「哦天，我能用这个做我们想办的那个大活动。我能用这个做一切。」

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: There's nothing off the table when you actually learn those fundamentals. But as well as I know smart people can learn that stuff. There's lots of resources out there. Reforge has some classes on it, there's a bunch of new product led growth classes out in the wild, like Maven I think has a couple. And there's a variety of those types of things that just going and doing it, you don't have to go and operate it yourself. You don't have to go become a product manager. But understanding those skills and those systems will, one, I think make you think differently about how to run your marketing team and, two, make you exponentially better at working with your product organization.
turns.zh: 当你真学了那些底层，没什么是不能碰的。而且我知道聪明人能学那些。外面很多资源。Reforge 有些课，外面有一堆新的产品驱动增长课，像 Maven 我想有几个。各种这类东西，去做了就行，你不必自己运作它。你不必去当产品经理。但理解那些技能那些系统，一，我觉得会让你用不同方式想怎么跑营销团队，二，让你指数级更好跟你的产品组织合作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I'm actually hearing from folks listening to this podcast not live right now, but broadly, that this is a good way to learn how product works and how product leaders think. So, that's interesting. So, if you're listening to this, good job. You also mentioned that a lot of marketing leaders don't work out at a company, they join, they leave, things go wrong. As a hiring founder or leader, what do you look for to tell you this person's probably not what we need and not what you'd call a Growth CMO? What are flags that are like they're probably not going to adapt and evolve to the way we want to operate?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我其实听到现在听这播客的人——不是直播——broadly，说这是学产品怎么运作、产品领导怎么想的好方式。所以那有意思。所以如果你在听这个，干得好。你也提到很多营销领导在公司不 work、他们加入、离开、出事。作为招聘的创始人或领导，你看什么来判断这人大概不是我们要的、不是你叫的增长型 CMO？有什么红旗说他们大概不会适应、演化成我们想运作的方式？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: So, I think first and foremost, it obviously depends on the stage. Anything let's say C or below, comfortable with chaos and willingness to go do something they have not done for probably 15 years are two huge signals for me, because every company I've been part of at every scale now, which is all of them basically, that's the thing that a lot of people coming from more traditional marketing environments into startup worlds, it's a pace and just the unpredictability and change and those kinds of things are just at such a higher rate than they've seen for a long time that it can be really jarring for people.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得首先，显然看阶段。任何 C 或以下，对混乱的舒适、和愿意去做他们大概 15 年没做过的事，对我而言是两个巨大信号，因为我现在参与的每个规模的公司、基本全是，那是很多从更传统营销环境进创业世界的人，那个节奏、还有不可预测和变化那些，比他们长期见的高得多，对人有真冲击。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: And I think it's totally reasonable. It's crazy, right? If anybody that's had the exposure on both sides. And then the willingness to go do the work. People are churning constantly and the challenges are different every week and those types of things. And so it's like every now and then you've got to go write an email or you've got to go open up Facebook and get into the weeds with it with your team, into the data of it and that type of stuff. And that's stuff that I don't want to do, personally, me. I'm past the point where I should be in Facebook.
turns.zh: 我觉得完全合理。很疯，对吧？任何两边都有 exposure 的人。然后是愿意去做那个工作。人们一直在流失、挑战每周不同那些。所以就像偶尔你得去写封邮件、或者你得去开 Facebook、跟团队进杂草里、进它的数据那些。而那些东西，我个人，我不想做。我过了该在 Facebook 里的点。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: But man, when I need to, I'm willing to, and I'll go get in the weeds with it and I'll use my time to just be like, "Look, we have to figure this out now." And I'm going to go do the things that I thought I was done with in my career. So, those are pretty big ones. I think then generally speaking, one of the exercises I like to take founders through when they're hiring a marketing leader is every marketer is going to have a T-shaped career.
turns.zh: 但哥们，当需要，我愿意，我会去进杂草里、用我的时间就「看，我们现在得搞清楚这个」。而我会去做那些我以为我职业生涯已经做完了的事。所以那些是挺大的。我觉得然后 generally，我带创始人招营销领导时喜欢做的一个练习是，每个营销人都会有个 T 型职业。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Everybody came from something they probably became awesome at and then over time just expanded their purview. So, for me it was mobile. I got into mobile. My first client ever was on Sun Microsystems early 2000s, getting Java developers to make apps for flip phones. So, I just knew digital mobile world really, really well before a lot of people did. But then eventually I'm like, "Great, now I'm running an entire digital marketing team. Now I'm running an entire marketing team. Now I'm getting into growth. Now I want to learn product," and I've expanded. And so typically it's going through that exercise of find out their T, find out their strength, and then spend time figuring out how they make up for those other things.
turns.zh: 每个人都来自他们大概变得超强、然后随时间扩展视野的东西。所以对我那是移动。我进移动。我的第一个客户是 2000 年代初的 Sun Microsystems，让 Java 开发者给翻盖手机做 app。所以我很早、比很多人早，就很懂数字移动世界。但最后我像「好，现在我跑整个数字营销团队。现在我跑整个营销团队。现在我进增长。现在我想学产品」，我扩张了。所以通常是过那个练习——找出他们的 T、找出他们的强项，然后花时间搞清楚他们怎么补上其他那些。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: So, for me, at Lambda school I ran our PR team for a while. I am not a PR person, but I make it a goal in my life to get to the valley of despair of the Dunning-Kruger effect, to be like, "Great, I just need to know how bad I am at PR," because if I still think I'm good at it, that's not a good place for me to be. But once I know how bad it is, I now know I need to go hire the right person to come in and I'm going to listen to them. I'm not going to assume that I'm smarter than them, and those types of things. And so I think the same thing with product questions and data questions and experimentation questions for this concept of a Growth CMO is like, well, somebody's coming from a world where they've not had to work really closely with the product team, spend time with them to figure out how they plan on adapting to that.
turns.zh: 所以对我，在 Lambda School 我有阵子跑我们的 PR 团队。我不是 PR 人，但我把人生目标设成到达 Dunning-Kruger 效应的绝望谷——像「好，我只需要知道我在 PR 上有多烂」，因为我还以为我擅长，那对我不是好位置。但一旦我知道有多烂，我现在知道我需要去招对的人进来、我会听他们的。我不会假设我比他们聪明，那些。所以我觉得产品问题、数据问题、实验问题对增长型 CMO 这个概念也一样——某人来自一个没跟产品团队紧密工作过的世界，花时间跟他们搞清楚他们计划怎么适应那个。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: My guess is most won't have thought of that. The good ones will be able to figure it out together with you in that interview, or afterwards, or whatever it might be.
turns.zh: 我猜大多没想过那个。好的那些会在面试里、或之后、或不管什么，能跟你一起搞清楚。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Maybe one day we'll do a follow-up chat just to dive into hiring a marketing person. I know that's a whole deep topic.
turns.zh: 太棒了。也许哪天我们做个跟进聊，专门深挖招营销人。我知道那是个深话题。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Lots of thoughts.
turns.zh: 很多想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Oh man. Okay. We've got to book that. But, okay. So, you mentioned the valley of despair, and that's a good segue to our next topic. So, I found this old tweet of yours where you talk about burnout and depression, and you kind of make this point that a lot of times you feel like it's burnout and it's actually depression. And just broadly mental health is just this topic that's not really spoken a lot about in tech and in business. And so I'd love to just spend a little time on this. I know you're a big proponent of talking about these sorts of things, so I'm curious, I know you've been through both these things and I'm curious just to hear your journey, what that's been like, and what you've learned about how to get through it?
turns.zh: 好。哦哥们。好。我们得约那个。但，好。你提到绝望谷，那是我们下一个话题的好过渡。我找到你一条旧推文，你聊倦怠和抑郁，你有点提出这点：很多时候你觉得是倦怠、其实它是抑郁。而 broadly 心理健康就是科技和生意里不太被谈的话题。所以我想花点时间在这。我知道你是聊这类事的大拥护者，所以我好奇，我知道你两方面都经历过，我好奇听你的旅程、那是什么样、和你学到怎么度过？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: So, the two biggest inputs for me in terms of really taking the time to understand my mental health, one is my wife, who's been a very strong proponent of mental health resources for everybody since I met her. And so just being able to learn from her and get exposure to, well, why is this important? What are the values of it? And seeing it pretty regularly of family members, or coworkers. Or it's like, oh man, I bet there's something deeper here that maybe is important for them to figure out.
turns.zh: 所以对我真正花时间理解我心理健康的两个最大输入，一是我老婆，她从认识起就是心理健康资源的强拥护者。所以能跟她学、接触到，哦，为啥这重要？它的价值是什么？而且挺规律地看到家庭成员、或同事。或者就像，哦哥们，我打赌这有更深的东西、也许对他们重要去搞清楚。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is that just something she's good at, or is she trained in this stuff?
turns.zh: 那是她就擅长，还是她受过这训练？

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: No, she's good at it and she's in therapy and stuff like that. She's one of the most empathetic, passionate people I've ever met in my life. And so she just feels like poor people so much that I think it's something really important to her. And then at Uber, I got to a spot where I was incredibly exhausted and tired and just down, not excited about work and things like that, and so I started going to therapy and with this assumption that I was just working too hard.
turns.zh: 不，她擅长、而且她在 therapy 之类。她是我这辈子见过最有同理心、最有热情的人之一。所以她对人的痛苦感受这么深，我觉得那对她真的很重要。然后在 Uber，我到一个点，极其疲惫、累、就低落，对工作不兴奋那些，所以我开始去 therapy，带着「我只是工作太狠」的假设。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: That was kind of my like, "Man, I need to go to therapy to figure out the tools that I need to deal with me working too hard." And I just uncovered so many interesting things that I wouldn't have expected. So, one was that I'm the youngest child in my family and I did something pretty different than a lot of my relatives and things like that. So, recognition is something I long for, and it turns out I get that at work and I just hadn't gotten that in other parts of my life. And so this thing that I'm like, "This is my problem," was actually a solution to my real problem.
turns.zh: 那有点像我的「哥们，我得去 therapy 搞清楚我要对付工作太狠需要的工具」。而我挖出这么多没想到的事。一是我是家里最小的孩子，我做了跟我很多亲戚挺不同的事那些。所以认可，是我渴望的东西，而结果我在工作里得到那个、而我在生活其他部分没得到。所以这件我以为「这是我的问题」的事，其实是我真实问题的解。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: And knowing that just helped me totally just change my perspective of how hard I work. I was getting judgemental about myself around, "Man, I'm working too hard. I shouldn't be doing this, but I have to." And then I got in the spot where I'm like, "Oh, I'm working hard because I love it, because I like it, I'm having an impact and I'm working with people I like and people respect the work that I do." And that helped me identify that I can work just as hard, but I can work smarter. I can work more on the things I have impact on.
turns.zh: 知道那个就帮我完全改变我对自己工作多狠的视角。我之前对自己审判「哥们，我工作太狠。我不该做这个，但我必须。」然后我到那个点「哦，我工作狠是因为我爱它、因为我喜欢、我有影响、我跟喜欢的人工作、人们尊重我做的工。」那帮我识别我能工作一样狠，但我能更聪明地工作。我能在我有影响的事上工作更多。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: I can work more with people that actually respected the type of work that I'm doing. And that actually just started to relax me and get me to the spot of, "Oh, okay," I still some burnout in there, and that's part of the innovation. Part of my title was that I got to a spot where I'm like, I was traveling constantly, I had teams all over the world and the structure of Uber was working where every city had a GM and I was the person they called when their spend was too high. And so 500 GMs-
turns.zh: 我能在真的尊重我做的工的种类的人上工作更多。而那其实就开始让我放松、到我「哦，好」的点，里面还有些倦怠，而那部分是创新。我头衔的一部分是我到一个点，我像，我一直在出差，我有全世界的团队、而且 Uber 的结构是每城市有个 GM、而我是他们花费太高时打电话的人。所以 500 个 GM——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Uber GMs especially.
turns.zh: 尤其 Uber 的 GM。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And so I was working in a world where I was dealing with a lot of politics. I love mentoring people, and I had this massive team of 150 people that I barely know any of them. And so I'm not mentoring people either anymore. And I just felt like I'm working so hard on things that I actually don't enjoy. And so I'm like, I'm going to go work on flying cars, which is a whole other podcast too. So, that was my, okay, there was burnout in there.
turns.zh: 对，正是。所以我在一个处理很多政治的世界工作。我爱 mentor 人，而我有这个 150 人的大团队、我几乎不认识任何一个。所以我也不再 mentor 人了。而我就是感觉我在这么狠地工作在我其实不享受的事上。所以我像，我要去搞飞行汽车，那是另一档播客。所以那是我，好，里面有倦怠。

turns.speaker: Adam Grenier
turns.en: I know that was a fact, but some of those feelings or things that I felt my entire life that I uncovered that I thought was just burnt out, I was like, "Oh, actually at this point in my life, this point in my life and this point in my life, I felt this way too. And at those points I wasn't burnt out. And so I actually have deeper work to do here and deeper understanding of myself so that I can actually maximize my life and enjoy it." And because I'm going to keep working to some degree this hard. And I want to just make the most of that.
turns.zh: 我知道那是事实，但我一生里感觉到的某些那些感觉、我以为只是倦怠挖出来的，我像「哦，其实在我人生的这个点、这个点、这个点，我也这么感觉过。而那些点我没倦怠。所以我其实有更深的工作要做、更深的自我理解，这样我能真最大化我的人生、享受它。」因为我会继续在某种程度工作这么狠。而我想就最大化那个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know if you mentioned this, but I imagine parts of those points were depression, not burnout. What have you found to be that line of just like, "Oh wow, this is a lot more serious than I'm just working way too hard?"
turns.zh: 我不知道你提没提，但我猜那些点有些部分是抑郁，不是倦怠。你发现那条线是什么、就像「哦哇，这比我只是工作太狠严重得多」？
